title: Romans say perfect/absolute in essence, not degree
source_text: XXVII. Hic autem certe tanta est veritatis evidentia, ut etiam qui verbis videntur con-tradicere, reipsa tamen idem dicere comperiantur. Nam Scholae Romanae Doctores plane quidem adversa Reformatis loquuntur. Nolunt enim justitiam per Spiritum Sanctum fide-libus infusam, inchoatam solum & imperfectam dici: & acriter contendunt illam esse, & dici debere, perfectam atque absolutam. Sed, quum mentem suam distinctius expli-cant, in eundem plane sensum cum Theologis Reformatis recidunt. Quippe quando justitiam, de qua agimus, absolutam vocant, non intelligunt talem esse ut pervenerit ad summum, & ei nihil addi possit. Et similiter, quum dicunt perfectam, non in-telligunt perfectam simpliciter, & talem cui nihil omnino desit. Fatentur enim justos in hac vita suos adhuc habere naevos, & in varia peccata incidere; non ita gravia quidem, ut propter illa justitia excidant, sed quae tamen egeant divina misericordia & condonatione. Et hominum etiam sanctissimorum docent justitiam esse ejusmodi, quae quotidie per-fici, & augmentum sumere possit. Itaque justitiam fidelium in hac vita propterea tan-tum absolutam vocant, quoniam absolute, simpliciter, & revera talis est: non vero tantum justitia quaedam improprie, secundum quid, & per aliquam fictionem sic di-cta. Et similiter illam perfectam vocant, quoniam illi nihil deest quod ad essentiam verae justitiae pertineat: licet desit illi quaedam perfectio accidentaria, & multis gra-dibus a summa perfectione absit.
pass_a_gloss: But here certainly the evidence of truth is so great that even those who seem to contradict in words are found in the thing itself to say the same. For the doctors of the Roman School speak indeed plainly opposite to the Reformed. For they are unwilling that the righteousness infused into believers by the Holy Spirit be called only begun and imperfect; and they sharply contend that it is, and ought to be called, perfect and absolute. But when they explain their mind more distinctly, they fall back into the very same sense with the Reformed theologians. For when they call the righteousness of which we treat absolute, they do not understand it to be such that it has reached the summit and nothing can be added to it. And likewise, when they say perfect, they do not understand perfect simply, and such that nothing at all is lacking to it. For they confess that the just in this life still have their blemishes and fall into various sins—not indeed so grave that they fall from righteousness on their account, but such as nevertheless need divine mercy and pardon. And they teach that the righteousness even of the most holy men is of such a kind that it can daily be perfected and take increase. Therefore they call the righteousness of believers in this life absolute only because it is absolutely, simply, and truly such—not merely a certain righteousness improperly, in a qualified sense, and by some fiction so called. And likewise they call it perfect because nothing is lacking to it that belongs to the essence of true righteousness; although a certain accidental perfection is lacking to it, and it is many degrees short of the highest perfection.
pass_b_english: Roman doctors verbally reject inchoate/imperfect language, calling it perfect and absolute—yet when explained, they mean essence, not degree.
They admit remaining blemishes and need of mercy; absolute = truly such, not fictively.
